While these error metrics can be readily computed with the help of labeled data, the reliability of such estimates depends on the accuracy of test labels, which may not always be perfect.
The F-Measure is a classification-oriented measure of cluster validity.
It is one of five measures commonly used to evaluate the performance of a classification model, alongside entropy, purity, precision, and recall.
A confusion matrix is a table used to evaluate the performance of a classifier by comparing predicted labels against true labels.

In the context of multi-class classification, the matrix generalizes the binary structure (which uses four counts: TP, FP, TN, FN) to an N x N grid where each entry denotes the number of instances from actual class i predicted to be of class j.

The matrix provides the information needed to determine how well a model performs, and these counts are often summarized into single-value metrics like accuracy (Number of correct predictions / Total number of predictions) to facilitate comparison between models.
accuracy (Number of correct predictions / Total number of predictions)
A confidence interval for accuracy quantifies the uncertainty of a classifier's measured accuracy by providing a plausible range for its true accuracy.
Because accuracy is calculated on a finite test set, the measured value is an estimate rather than the exact true performance.

The estimation approach models the classification task as a binomial random experiment consisting of N independent trials, where each trial has two possible outcomes (success or failure) and the probability of success, p, is constant.
Under the normal approximation, the confidence interval is calculated as the estimate plus or minus an uncertainty margin.
The uncertainty margin is defined as Z_{1-α/2} multiplied by the square root of p(1-p)/N, where Z_{1-α/2} is the critical value corresponding to the chosen confidence level.
For example, a 95% confidence level corresponds to a Z-value of 1.96.
In a specific case, a model with 80% accuracy evaluated on 100 test instances yields a 95% confidence interval between 71.1% and 86.7%.
This method is distinct from testing the statistical significance of the observed deviation between two different models, which is a separate issue in model comparison.

Comparing Two Models on Independent Test Sets is a statistical evaluation procedure used to determine whether the observed performance difference between two distinct models is statistically significant.
This unit applies specifically when two models, denoted M1 and M2, are evaluated on two independent test sets, D1 and D2.
The setup requires that the data used for model selection be kept separate from the data used for model evaluation to ensure a clean evaluation setup.
In this context, n1 represents the number of instances in test set D1, and n2 represents the number of instances in test set D2.
The error rate for model M1 on test set D1 is denoted as e1, and the error rate for model M2 on test set D2 is denoted as e2.
The primary goal of this comparison is to test whether the observed difference between e1 and e2 is statistically significant, rather than merely a result of random variation in the test data.
The significance level, denoted by the Greek letter alpha (α), is a user-defined threshold used to determine whether a statistical result is significant.
A result is considered statistically significant if its associated p-value is lower than the chosen significance level.
Common choices for this threshold include 0.05 (5%) and 0.01 (1%).
The significance level is used to decide whether one model is significantly better than another; for example, a Z-statistic may be compared against a threshold derived from a 5% significance level.
The p-value of a statistically significant result represents the probability of falsely rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true.

In multiple hypothesis testing scenarios, the significance level may be adjusted to control the family-wise error rate; for instance, the Bonferroni procedure uses a modified significance level of α/m, where m is the number of results, while the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure balances the overly conservative Bonferroni approach and the overly liberal naive approach by allowing the significance level to grow linearly up to α.
Without careful consideration of these evaluation issues, data mining results may be false discoveries, lacking meaningfulness or reproducibility.
one-sided and two-sided tests are distinguished by how the probability mass of the null distribution is allocated to the tails

One-sided tests are categorized into right-tailed and left-tailed variants, where the entire probability mass associated with the significance level is concentrated in a single tail of the distribution
a two-sided test splits this probability mass equally between both tails of the null distribution
when a significance level of 0.05 is used, a one-sided test places all 0.05 probability in one tail, whereas a two-sided test places 0.025 probability in each of the two tails
This distinction determines how p-values are calculated as the area in the tails of the null distribution
This distinction is applied when checking for differences between models, such as comparing the error rates of two different models on test instances
An ensemble classifier is a technique for improving classification accuracy by aggregating the predictions of multiple base classifiers, also known as classifier combination methods.
The core idea is to construct a set of base classifiers from training data and perform classification by taking a vote on the predictions made by each base classifier.
ensemble methods tend to perform better than any single classifier, as the combined decision can be more robust even when individual base classifiers are imperfect.
For classification, a common combination rule is majority voting, where the final prediction is determined by the majority of the base classifiers' outputs.

The ensemble can be constructed in various ways, including by manipulating the training set through resampling or by manipulating the input features by choosing subsets of features for each training set.

Empirical comparisons show that ensemble classifiers generally outperform a single decision tree classifier on many data sets, with methods like bagging, boosting, and random forests using base classifiers such as decision trees.
Majority voting is a combination rule used in ensemble classification to produce a final prediction from the outputs of multiple base classifiers.
each base classifier predicts a class for a given test instance, and the class that receives the most votes becomes the final ensemble prediction.
This method is commonly applied in random forests, where the final prediction for classification tasks is determined by majority vote, while regression tasks use averaging.
while individual base classifiers may be imperfect, their combined decision can be more robust and reliable, particularly when the models make different mistakes.
ŷ = majority{h₁(x), h₂(x), ..., hB(x)}, where x is the test instance, hb is the b-th base classifier, B is the number of base classifiers, and ŷ is the final ensemble prediction.
In the specific context of binary classification with labels -1 and +1, taking the majority vote is equivalent to summing up the predicted values of y and examining the sign of the resulting sum.
Majority voting is distinguished from weighted majority voting, where the weight of a base classifier denotes its accuracy or relevance, and from the averaging rule used in regression.

It is a standard component of ensemble methods such as bagging and random forests, where it helps control overfitting and improves generalization compared to relying on a single high-variance classifier.
A random forest is an ensemble method that uses decision trees as its base classifiers.
It is designed to improve generalization performance by constructing an ensemble of decorrelated decision trees.
The method builds on the idea of bagging by using a different bootstrap sample of the training data for learning each decision tree.

A key distinguishing feature of random forests from bagging is that at every internal node of a tree, the best splitting criterion is chosen among a small set of randomly selected attributes, rather than considering all attributes.

The basic procedure of training a random forest classifier involves the following steps: 1. Construct a bootstrap sample of the training set by randomly sampling n instances (with replacement) from the training set D. 2. Grow a decision tree using the bootstrap sample, where at each internal node, a random subset of attributes is selected and the best split is chosen among that subset. 3. Repeat the process to build many decision trees. 4. For classification, the final random-forest predictionis

Random forests do not need to use a separate partition of the training set for validation, as it can simultaneously train the base classifiers and compute generalization error estimates on the same data set.

Random forests have been empirically found to provide significant improvements in generalization performance that are often comparable, if not superior, to the improvements provided by the AdaBoost algorithm.
Random forests are also more robust to overfitting and run much faster than the AdaBoost algorithm.
In a random forest, at each node: 1. choose a random subset of features, 2. evaluate candidate splits only among those selected features, 3. choose the best split from that subset.
For example, if there are d total features, the algorithm might consider only m features at each split, where m < d.
A common classification choice is approximately: m ≈ √ d.
The randomness makes the trees diverse.
The forest combines their predictions by majority vote, which usually generalizes better than relying on one high-variance tree.
Boosting is an ensemble learning method that constructs a final classifier by sequentially aggregating base classifiers obtained from multiple boosting rounds.

A defining characteristic of the process is its adaptive focus on difficult data: as the rounds proceed, examples that are the hardest to classify tend to become more prevalent in the selection process.
This occurs because examples that were not chosen in a previous round—often because their predictions were likely wrong—have a better chance of being selected in the next round.
The final ensemble is obtained by aggregating the base classifiers from each boosting round.

Over the years, several implementations of the boosting algorithm have been developed, which differ primarily in how the weights of training examples are updated at the end of each round and how the predictions made by each classifier are combined.

Notable implementations include AdaBoost, developed by Freund and Schapire, and Arcing, a variant proposed by Breiman that uses non-uniform weights assigned to training examples to resample the data for building an ensemble of training sets.
Empirical comparisons indicate that ensemble classifiers, including boosting, generally outperform a single decision tree classifier on many data sets.
Class imbalance, also known as skew, is a property of data sets where there is a disproportionate number of instances belonging to different classes.

A typical example is a health-care application using diagnostic reports to detect a rare disease, where the infrequent nature of the condition results in a smaller number of positively diagnosed subjects.
This imbalance poses two primary challenges for classification.

First, it is difficult to find sufficiently many labeled samples of the rare class; while some classifiers like rule-based methods and k-NN are more effective at handling imbalance than others, all are impacted if the minority class is not well-represented in the training set.
Second, accuracy, the traditional measure for evaluating classification performance, is not well-suited for evaluating models when the test data is imbalanced.
To address these issues, various methods exist for building classifiers on imbalanced training sets and for evaluating performance on skewed test sets.

These include sampling-based methods, algorithms specifically developed for mining rare classes such as SMOTE, PNrule, and CREDOS, and alternative evaluation metrics like precision, recall, the F1-measure, and ROC analysis.

Oversampling (SMOTE), formally known as the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique, is an alternative approach for oversampling designed to address class imbalance by generating synthetic positive instances in the neighborhood of existing positive instances.
This method is used to overcome the limitations of standard oversampling techniques.

The procedure for SMOTE consists of three ordered steps: first, determine the k-nearest positive neighbors of every positive instance; second, generate a synthetic positive instance at some intermediate point along the line segment joining a positive instance to one of its randomly chosen k-nearest neighbors; and third, repeat this generation process until the desired number of positive instances is reached.

SMOTE is categorized as an algorithm developed for mining rare classes and is distinct from other sampling-based methods for imbalanced data sets, such as PNrule and CREDOS, as well as from undersampling approaches.
Undersampling is a technique used to address class imbalance by transforming the training set so that both classes have nearly equal representation.

The primary goal is to overcome the skew among classes by selecting a random sample of examples from the majority class (the negative class) and using them with the existing examples from the minority class (the positive class) to create a balanced training set.
A classifier built over this resultant balanced set is intended to be unbiased toward both classes.
some useful negative examples, particularly those closer to the actual decision boundary, may not be chosen for training, which can result in an inferior classification model.
This approach is distinct from oversampling, which involves adding examples to the minority class rather than removing them from the majority class.

A cost matrix is a framework used in model evaluation to determine the best classifier by minimizing expected cost under the given cost matrix, rather than relying solely on metrics like the highest true positive rate or the lowest false positive rate.
This approach is particularly relevant in the context of class imbalance, where the real consequences of each type of decision vary.

The cost matrix allows for a cost-sensitive setting where the best model is the one that minimizes expected cost, which can differ from models that perform best by other metrics such as ROC/AUC or F1 at a specific threshold.
For example, in a cost-sensitive setting, a model with a lower expected cost may be preferred over one with higher performance on other metrics.

The cost matrix is distinct from the confusion matrix, which is a basic approach for representing a classifier's performance on a test set, and from the precision-recall curve, which is an alternate approach for measuring aggregate performance, especially useful in the presence of class imbalance.
The properties of a cost matrix have been studied in the literature, and it is a key concept in cost-sensitive learning.
Cost-Sensitive Classification is a concept within the domain of Data Mining, specifically under Model Evaluation and Model Comparison and the sub-topic of Class Imbalance.
It is associated with cost-sensitive learning, for which a tutorial is provided in a review article by Ling and Sheng.
The approach involves the use of a cost matrix, the properties of which were studied by C. Elkan in 'The Foundations of Cost-Sensitive Learning' (1997).
This method is relevant in the context of class imbalance, where alternative performance measures like the precision-recall (PR) curve are also utilized.
RIPPER is a widely-used rule induction algorithm that extracts rules directly from data using the sequential covering algorithm.
It is particularly suited for building models from data sets with imbalanced class distributions
and works well with noisy data because it uses a validation set to prevent model overfitting.
The algorithm scales almost linearly with the number of training instances.

The ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) curve is a graphical tool for aggregate evaluation that displays the trade-off between the True Positive Rate (TPR) and the False Positive Rate (FPR) of a classifier across varying score thresholds.
In this plot, the TPR is positioned on the y-axis and the FPR on the x-axis.
Each point on the curve represents a specific operating point of the classifier, generated by applying a particular threshold to the test scores.
The TPR is calculated as the ratio of true positives to the sum of true positives and false negatives, while the FPR is the ratio of false positives to the sum of false positives and true negatives.

The generic procedure for computing an ROC curve involves sorting test instances in increasing order of their scores, selecting the lowest-ranked instance, and assigning it and all higher-ranked instances to the positive class.
This initial step is equivalent to classifying all test instances as positive.
By varying the threshold, the curve facilitates the comparison of classifiers over a range of operating points, allowing selection based on application requirements.
ROC analysis is robust to specific threshold choices and was originally used in signal detection theory.
However, it is not suitable for measuring the impact of class skew, as different datasets with varying skew can produce identical ROC curves.
The area under the ROC curve (AUC) is a common summary metric, where a perfect classifier yields an AUC of 1 and random guessing yields 0.5, though AUC has known limitations.

ROC Space (TPR vs. FPR) is the two-dimensional coordinate system used to visualize the performance of a classifier, defined by the True Positive Rate (TPR) on the vertical axis and the False Positive Rate (FPR) on the horizontal axis.
The TPR is calculated as the fraction of actual positive instances correctly predicted as positive, expressed as TP / (TP + FN).
The FPR is calculated as the fraction of actual negative instances incorrectly predicted as positive, expressed as FP / (FP + TN).
Each point in this space represents a specific operating point of the classifier, generated by applying a particular threshold to the test scores produced by the model.
As the threshold varies, the classifier moves through this space, creating a curve that displays the trade-off between TPR and FPR.
A key characteristic of this space is that the TPR monotonically increases as the FPR increases, resulting in a staircase pattern for the curve.

The space contains critical reference points: the origin (0,0) represents a model that predicts every instance as negative; the point (1,1) represents a model that predicts every instance as positive; and the point (1,0) represents a perfect model with zero misclassifications.

A good classification model is located as close as possible to the upper-left corner of the diagram, while a model that makes random guesses resides along the main diagonal connecting the origin to the point (1,1).
ROC Space is agnostic to the skew in the test set because both TPR and FPR are invariant to class imbalance; consequently, the same ROC curve is obtained for test data sets with very different skew.
This property makes ROC Space unsuitable for measuring the impact of skew on classification performance, though it is useful for comparing classifiers over a range of operating points.
The Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) is a commonly used measure designed to summarize the aggregate behavior of a classifier across all operating points.

This metric is particularly useful when comparing classifiers that do not strictly dominate one another, meaning neither classifier consistently shows higher true positive rates and lower false positive rates across all thresholds.
AUC provides a single scalar value to evaluate overall performance: a perfect classifier yields an AUC of 1, while an algorithm that performs random guessing yields an AUC of 0.5.

A key property of the AUC is that it is insensitive to class skew in the test set, distinguishing it from other metrics like the area under the Precision-Recall curve (AUC-PR), which varies with changing skew.

Although AUC is a useful summary of aggregate performance, it has limitations; specifically, it can be used to compare the quality of two classifiers only if the ROC curve of one classifier strictly dominates the other.
In the context of ROC analysis and model evaluation, the classification threshold (also known as the cutoff) is a specific value used to determine model predictions.
It serves as the basis for computing performance metrics such as precision, recall, and F-measure.
Different threshold values (e.g., 0.5 and 0.1) can be compared to assess model performance, and the choice of threshold may depend on specific use cases or cost-sensitive evaluation criteria.
The ROC curve can be used to evaluate whether a particular threshold is optimal.

The threshold effect on precision, recall, and F1 describes how the choice of a classification threshold determines the final hard predictions from a model's scores, which in turn dictates the calculated values for precision, recall, and F1.
Precision, recall, and F1 are metrics that evaluate the final predictions after a specific threshold has been chosen.
Changing the threshold alters the balance between catching positive cases and creating false positives.
A threshold of 0.5 is characterized as conservative, while a threshold of 0.1 is characterized as aggressive.
Comparing these different thresholds demonstrates how the threshold choice directly changes precision, recall, false positives, and false negatives.

For example, in a specific model evaluation, a threshold of 0.5 yielded a precision of 0.750, a recall of 0.600, and an F1 of 0.667, whereas a threshold of 0.1 yielded a precision of 0.556, a recall of 1.000, and an F1 of 0.714.
The optimal threshold is not automatically defined by the ROC curve; rather, it depends on the specific goal, such as maximizing F1, minimizing cost, or reducing false positives.
This threshold selection process is distinct from ROC and AUC, which evaluate the model's scores across all possible thresholds rather than just at a single point like 0.5.
The holdout method is the most basic technique for partitioning a labeled data set to estimate model performance.
In this approach, the labeled set D is randomly partitioned into two disjoint sets: a training set (D.train) and a test set (D.test).
A classification model is induced from the training set, and its error rate on the test set is used as an estimate of the generalization error rate.

This method is distinguished from other evaluation techniques by its use of a single split, whereas random subsampling repeats the holdout process, and cross-validation ensures every instance is tested once.
The holdout method can be repeated several times to obtain a distribution of test error rates, an approach known as random subsampling or the repeated holdout method.
This repetition produces a distribution of error rates that can be used to understand the variance of the estimated error.
Random subsampling, also known as the repeated holdout method, is a model evaluation technique that repeats the holdout method several times to obtain a distribution of test error rates.
In each repetition, the data is randomly split into training and test sets, the classifier is trained on the training set, evaluated on the test set, and the performance is recorded.
After multiple repetitions, the results are averaged.
This method produces a distribution of error rates that can be used to understand the variance of the test error.
Random subsampling reduces dependence on a single split but is more computationally expensive than a single holdout split.
Unlike cross-validation, random subsampling does not guarantee that each instance is tested exactly once, and some instances may never appear in the test set.
k-Fold Cross Validation is a model evaluation method that divides a labeled dataset into k approximately equal parts, or folds.

The procedure consists of four ordered steps: first, split the data into k folds; second, for each fold i, use fold i as the test set and the other k − 1 folds as the training set; third, train and test k times; and fourth, average the k performance scores.
The final score is calculated as the sum of the performance of each fold divided by k.
A key advantage of this method is that each instance is used for testing exactly once and for training k − 1 times, which makes effective use of all labeled instances for both training and testing.
However, the method produces a single estimate of the generalization error rate without providing information about the variance of that estimate.
Additionally, results can still depend somewhat on how the folds are formed, and if data has groups, time ordering, or leakage risks, ordinary random folds may be inappropriate.

In k-fold cross-validation, a different model is learned at every run, and the performance of every one of the k models on their respective test folds is aggregated to compute the overall test error rate.
This aggregated rate does not reflect the generalization error rate of any single one of the k models.
An empirical study by Kohavi suggests that the best estimation method is ten-fold, stratified cross-validation.

The original cross-validation method was proposed independently by Allen, Stone, and Geisser for model assessment, and its usage for model selection is quite different than when it is used for model evaluation.
Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) is a special case of k-fold cross-validation where the number of folds k equals the total number of instances N in the dataset.
In this approach, each fold contains exactly one test instance.
The procedure is repeated for every instance in the dataset: for each instance, the classifier is trained on the other N − 1 instances and tested on the single left-out instance.
This process is repeated until every instance has been left out once.
LOOCV is considered an extreme case of cross-validation that utilizes as much data as possible for training, which reduces the bias in the estimate of generalization error rate.
It can be computationally expensive for large datasets because the cross-validation procedure needs to be repeated N times.
Additionally, because there is only one possible partitioning for the leave-one-out approach, it is not possible to estimate the variance of the generalization error rate.
Individual test results can be highly variable because each test set has only one instance, and the method can produce misleading results in some special scenarios.
It is not always better than ordinary k-fold cross-validation in practice.
Bootstrap sampling is a model evaluation technique that creates training sets by sampling instances from the original dataset with replacement.

In this process, an instance previously selected to be part of the training set is equally likely to be drawn again, meaning some instances may appear several times in the same training set while others may be omitted.
Each bootstrap sample has the same size as the original data.
a bootstrap sample contains about 63.2% unique instances on average, leaving about 36.8% of the instances available for out-of-bag testing in each repetition

Bootstrap sampling is useful for small datasets and repeated estimates, and it is used to compute distributions of measures of classification performance, such as accuracy, precision, and recall, as well as to estimate the distribution of the support of a frequent itemset.
These distributions can be used to produce confidence intervals for these measures.
The bootstrap method was presented by Efron in 1979.
For classification, an alternative to bootstrap sampling is k-fold cross-validation, where the data set is systematically split into subsets for k number of times.
Bootstrap sampling has the main weakness of duplicate training cases and less intuitive interpretation compared to other methods.
Stratified k-fold cross-validation is a model evaluation technique defined as k-fold cross-validation where each fold approximately preserves the class proportions of the original dataset.
the dataset is divided into k approximately equal parts called folds.
For each fold, that specific fold is used as the test set while the remaining k-1 folds are used as the training set.
This process is repeated k times so that each fold is used once for testing.
The final performance estimate is calculated by averaging the k performance scores obtained from these runs.
This method is especially useful for imbalanced classification problems because it reduces evaluation instability caused by unlucky class distributions.
it still requires multiple model trainings and does not solve all leakage problems; if the data has time or group structure, stratification alone may be insufficient.
Empirical studies suggest that ten-fold stratified cross-validation is a highly effective estimation method for model evaluation.
Feature selection is the process of choosing an optimal subset of features according to a criterion.
Formally, given an original feature set F = {f1, f2, ..., fd}, where d is the number of features, feature selection aims to find a subset S such that S ⊆ F.
The criterion determines the details of evaluating feature subsets, and the selection of the criterion must be done according to the purposes of feature selection.
For example, an optimal subset could be a minimal subset that could give the best estimate of predictive accuracy.
Generally, the objective of feature selection is to identify the features in the data set which are important, and discard others as redundant or irrelevant.
Feature selection is a basic data preprocessing technique, especially after the year 2000, and is one of the most commonly used techniques for dimensionality and data reduction.

The feature selection process is viewed as consisting of four parts: a measure for evaluating a subset, a search strategy that controls the generation of a new subset of features, a stopping criterion, and a validation procedure.
Conceptually, feature subset selection is a search over all possible subsets of features.
Many different types of search strategies can be used, but the search strategy should be computationally inexpensive and should find optimal or near optimal sets of features.
It is usually not possible to satisfy both requirements, and thus, trade-offs are necessary.
There are three standard approaches to feature selection: embedded, filter, and wrapper.
Embedded approaches occur naturally as part of the data mining algorithm, where the algorithm itself decides which attributes to use and which to ignore.
Filter methods and wrapper methods differ only in the way in which they evaluate a subset of features.
For a wrapper method, subset evaluation uses the target data mining algorithm, while for a filter approach, the evaluation technique is distinct from the target data mining algorithm.

While some irrelevant and redundant attributes can be eliminated immediately by using common sense or domain knowledge, selecting the best subset of features frequently requires a systematic approach.
The ideal approach to feature selection is to try all possible subsets of features as input to the data mining algorithm of interest, and then take the subset that produces the best results.
This method has the advantage of reflecting the objective and bias of the data mining algorithm that will eventually be used.
Unfortunately, since the number of subsets involving n attributes is 2^n, such an approach is impractical in most situations and alternative strategies are needed.
Redundant features are input attributes that duplicate much or all of the information contained in one or more other attributes.
An attribute is considered redundant when it can be derived from another attribute or a set of them, or when it is strongly correlated with another attribute in the data.
the purchase price of a product and the amount of sales tax paid contain much of the same information

Redundancy is a problem that should be avoided as much as possible because it usually causes an increment in the data set size, meaning that the modeling time of data mining algorithms is incremented as well, and may also induce overfitting in the obtained model.
Redundant and irrelevant features can reduce classification accuracy and the quality of the clusters that are found.
Inconsistencies in dimension or attribute names can cause redundancies as well.
The objective of feature selection is to identify the features in the data set which are important, and discard others as redundant or irrelevant.
While some redundant attributes can be eliminated immediately by using common sense or domain knowledge, selecting the best subset of features frequently requires a systematic approach.
Inter-feature redundancy can be assessed by measuring association or correlation between pairs of selected features.
For numerical features, Pearson correlation is used, which measures linear relationship.
For ordinal features, Spearman correlation is used.
For categorical features, the chi-squared test is used.
For Pearson and Spearman, the range is [−1, 1].
For redundancy, 0 is ideal and ±1 is catastrophic.
The basic principle of redundancy reduction is to remove those features carrying little or no additional information beyond that subsumed by the rest of features.

In decision tree algorithms, redundant attributes show similar gains in purity if they are selected for splitting, so only one of them will be selected as an attribute test condition, meaning decision trees can handle the presence of redundant attributes.
Irrelevant features are defined as attributes that contain almost no useful information for the specific data mining task at hand.
This concept is distinguished from redundant features, which duplicate much or all of the information contained in one or more other attributes.
A concrete example of an irrelevant feature is a student's ID number, which is irrelevant to the task of predicting students' grade point averages.
In contrast, redundant features are exemplified by the purchase price of a product and the amount of sales tax paid, which contain much of the same information.
The presence of irrelevant features, along with redundant features, can reduce classification accuracy and the quality of the clusters that are found.
While some irrelevant attributes can be eliminated immediately by using common sense or domain knowledge, selecting the best subset of features frequently requires a systematic approach.
The ideal approach to feature selection is to try all possible subsets of features as input to the data mining algorithm of interest, and then take the subset that produces the best results.
This method has the advantage of reflecting the objective and bias of the data mining algorithm that will eventually be used.
The curse of dimensionality refers to the phenomenon that many types of data analysis become significantly harder as the dimensionality of the data increases.
This phenomenon is identified as a serious obstacle to the competence of most learning algorithms, especially because they are usually computationally expensive.

The curse of dimensionality is a distinct concept from the techniques used to address it; for example, feature selection is an effective form of dealing with dimensionality reduction by selecting attributes that are a subset of the old attributes, whereas dimensionality reduction is often reserved for techniques that create new attributes that are a combination of the old attributes.
Reducing dimensionality generally reduces the amount of time and memory required by data mining algorithms, improving the analysis with respect to time, cost, and quality.
The Filter Approach is a method for feature subset selection in which the evaluation technique used to assess a subset of features is distinct from the target data mining algorithm.

Within the common architecture for feature subset selection, the process consists of four parts: a measure for evaluating a subset, a search strategy that controls the generation of a new subset of features, a stopping criterion, and a validation procedure.

Filter methods and wrapper methods differ only in the way in which they evaluate a subset of features; for a filter approach, the evaluation is independent of the target algorithm, whereas for a wrapper method, subset evaluation uses the target data mining algorithm as a black box.
Because embedded approaches are algorithm-specific, the filter and wrapper approaches are the primary methods discussed in this context.

The Filter Approach is distinguished from the Wrapper Approach by this separation of evaluation from the target algorithm, and it is distinct from the Ranker (Filter Subcategory), which is a specific implementation within the filter family.
The Wrapper Approach is a feature selection strategy that uses the target data mining algorithm as a black box to find the best subset of attributes.
Unlike filter methods, which evaluate features before learning using a distinct criterion, wrapper methods evaluate candidate subsets by training and testing the learner itself.
This approach is one of three standard methods for feature selection, alongside filter and embedded approaches.

The feature selection process generally consists of four parts: a measure for evaluating a subset, a search strategy that controls the generation of new subsets, a stopping criterion, and a validation procedure.

Wrapper methods differ from filter methods specifically in how they evaluate a subset: for wrappers, the evaluation uses the target data mining algorithm, whereas for filters, the evaluation technique is distinct from the target algorithm.
Wrapper approaches are typically used when the goal is to find the best subset of attributes without enumerating all possible subsets, which is impractical for large numbers of attributes.
However, wrapper approaches require higher computational costs compared to filter methods, as they involve training and testing the learner for each candidate subset.
This makes them suitable for domains where the computational cost can be managed and the classifier is compatible with the wrapper approach.
The trade-off between filter and wrapper approaches in feature selection is defined by how the selection process is connected to the learning algorithm.

Both approaches operate within a common architecture consisting of four parts: a measure for evaluating a subset, a search strategy that controls the generation of new subsets, a stopping criterion, and a validation procedure.

The fundamental difference lies in the evaluation measure: filter methods use an evaluation technique that is distinct from the target data mining algorithm, whereas wrapper methods use the target data mining algorithm itself as a black box to evaluate candidate subsets.
In practice, filter methods evaluate features before learning occurs, while wrapper methods evaluate subsets by training and testing the learner.
Wrapper approaches typically do not enumerate all possible subsets, but they require higher computational costs than filter approaches.
Wrapper methods are considered an interesting choice in some domains, provided they can be applied with the same classifiers and the higher computational costs are taken into account.
Embedded approaches are excluded from this comparison because they are algorithm-specific.
Sequential Forward Generation (SFG) is a feature selection search strategy that begins with an empty set of features, denoted as S.
The search proceeds by iteratively adding features to S based on a criterion that distinguishes the best feature from the others.
The set S grows until it reaches a full set of original features.
The stopping criteria for SFG can be a threshold for the number of relevant features, denoted as m, or the generation of all possible subsets in brute force mode.
SFG is one of two primary directions of search in feature selection, the other being Sequential Backward Generation (SBG), which starts with a full set and removes features.
SFG is distinguished from SBG by its additive nature, starting from an empty set and adding features, whereas SBG is subtractive, starting from a full set and removing features.

SFG is also distinct from other search strategies such as Random Generation (RG), Bidirectional Generation (BG), Exhaustive Search, Heuristic Search, and Non-Deterministic Search, which have different search mechanisms and criteria.
Sequential Backward Generation (SBG) is a heuristic feature selection method that constructs a feature subset by iteratively removing features from the full set.
The algorithm begins with the complete feature set, denoted as F.
At each step, a selection criterion identifies the next worst or least relevant feature, f, which is then removed from the current set.
This process continues until the remaining set no longer satisfies the specified criterion or until the set becomes empty.
Upon termination, the algorithm returns the set of features that existed immediately before the final removal, effectively adding the last removed feature back to the set.
This recovery step ensures that the returned subset is the last acceptable configuration that met the evaluation criteria.

SBG is distinguished from Sequential Forward Generation (SFG), which builds a subset by adding features from an empty set, and from Bidirectional Generation (BG), which combines both forward and backward search strategies.
Unlike Random Generation (RG), which is non-deterministic, SBG is a deterministic heuristic search.
Bidirectional Generation (BG) is a heuristic feature selection method that combines forward and backward search strategies.
It operates by running Sequential Forward Generation (SFG) and Sequential Backward Generation (SBG) concurrently.
One side of the search builds up a feature set from an empty starting point, while the other side removes features from the full feature set.
The algorithm stops when either the forward or backward search finds a satisfactory subset.
This approach is used because the optimal number of features is usually unknown, making it impossible to determine in advance which single-direction scheme would be faster.
By searching from both ends, the probability of finding the optimal subset is increased, as a search in one direction usually finishes faster than in the other.
The algorithm takes as input the full feature set and a measure function, and returns the first satisfactory subset found by either direction.
Random Generation (RG) is a feature subset generation method that operates by generating random subsets of features rather than following a fixed, deterministic search path.
It is characterized as non-deterministic because the specific subsets produced depend on random choices.
The algorithm takes as input the full feature set and a utility measure, and it initializes both the current subset and the best subset found so far as empty sets.
The core mechanism involves making random decisions to either add or remove features from the current subset.
This approach is designed to avoid stagnation in local optima by not pursuing a particular fixed direction for subset generation.
When the stopping criterion is reached, the algorithm returns the best satisfactory subset found during the search process.

RG is one of several feature selection strategies, distinct from Sequential Forward Generation (SFG), Sequential Backward Generation (SBG), and Bidirectional Generation (BG), which rely on systematic forward or backward search directions.
Exhaustive search is a feature subset construction method that covers the entire search space by generating all non-empty subsets of the available features.
The set of subsets generated is the power set of the feature set F, excluding the empty set: P(F) - {∅}.
This approach is distinguished from heuristic and non-deterministic search methods, which do not evaluate the complete space.
In the context of feature selection, exhaustive search is often considered more interpretable because the retained features maintain their original meaning.

The method can be implemented using forward or backward search strategies, where the subset of features is gradually grown or reduced, respectively, with an evaluation measure that must be satisfied at each step.
Exhaustive search is one of the primary search categories presented in feature selection lectures, alongside heuristic and non-deterministic search.
Heuristic search is a category of feature selection strategy that seeks a good trade-off between the optimality of the selected feature subset and the quantity of computational resources required.
It is one of three main search categories, alongside exhaustive search and non-deterministic search.
Heuristic methods generally do not expect to find the globally optimal subset; instead, they aim to find a rapid solution that is closer to an optimal one.
This approach is particularly useful because it is usually not possible to satisfy both the requirements of being computationally inexpensive and finding the optimal set of features simultaneously.

The simplest heuristic method involves learning a model and selecting the features used by the data mining algorithm, provided the algorithm allows this, such as with decision trees or artificial neural networks.
Heuristic search is distinguished from exhaustive search, which generates all non-empty subsets, and from non-deterministic search, which relies on random generation.

Non-deterministic search, also known as stochastic search, is a feature selection strategy that adds or removes features to and from a subset without a sequential order, allowing the search to follow feature subsets that are randomly generated.
This approach is one of three main categories of search strategies used to find a good trade-off between optimality and the quantity of resources required.
The primary algorithm associated with this category is Random feature set generation (RG).

The RG algorithm takes the full feature set and a measure as inputs, initializes the current subset and the best subset as empty, and operates by generating random subsets, testing them against the measure, and keeping the best subset until a stopping condition is met.
The non-deterministic nature of RG arises specifically because the generated subsets are random.

In the taxonomy of feature selection algorithms, non-deterministic search is paired with evaluation measures such as Probability, Consistency, and Accuracy, corresponding to algorithm categories C13, C14, and C15.
This strategy contrasts with exhaustive search, which generates all non-empty subsets, and heuristic search, which uses sequential forward or backward generation.

Shannon entropy is a standard uncertainty function used to measure class impurity or uncertainty at a node in decision tree learning.

It quantifies the uncertainty of a receiver when receiving a message; if the receiver understands the message, the associated uncertainty is low, but if the receiver is not able to completely understand the message, all messages have almost equal probability of being received and the uncertainty increases.
In the context of feature selection and decision trees, entropy serves as the impurity measure behind information gain.

The p-value is the conditional probability of observing a particular value of a test statistic, R, or something more extreme under the null hypothesis.
Computing the p-value requires assuming the null hypothesis is true, and it measures how compatible the observed result is with that hypothesis.
A low p-value indicates that a result at least as extreme as the observed result is less likely to be obtained from the null hypothesis.
The level of significance, denoted by α, is a user-defined threshold on p-values.
A result is called statistically significant if it has a p-value lower than α.
The p-value of a statistically significant result denotes the probability of falsely rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true.
Common choices for the level of significance are 0.05 (5%) and 0.01 (1%).

One-sided tests, also referred to as right-tailed or left-tailed tests, are used when the alternative hypothesis specifies a directional relationship, such as a parameter being greater than or less than a null value
a two-sided test is used when the alternative hypothesis allows for a difference in either direction, without specifying whether the parameter is greater or smaller
The distinction between these test types is fundamentally reflected in how the p-value is calculated from the null distribution

For a two-sided test, the total probability mass associated with the significance level is split equally between the two tails; for example, with a 0.05 significance level, 0.025 probability is allocated to each tail
a one-sided test concentrates the entire probability mass of the significance level into a single tail, meaning all 0.05 probability is located in one tail
